entries.title: What SMPL is
entries.answer: SMPL.ai is a Financial Intelligence platform built specifically for SaaS companies. It works alongside the accounting system, CRM, HR, and billing platforms a finance team already uses, and automates the work of collecting, reconciling, analyzing, and explaining financial data — delivering executive-ready reporting in minutes after close, with the evidence behind every number.

entries.title: Not a dashboard / BI tool
topics: how is this different from BI
isn't this just a BI tool
keywords: how is this different from bi
isn't this just a bi tool
entries.answer: It isn't a dashboard and it isn't a system of record. It's the decision-support layer that sits above the systems of record — the layer every SaaS finance team currently rebuilds by hand in spreadsheets every month. A BI tool lets you drill from a summary toward more granular numbers within one system; our lineage runs all the way to the original source record, whichever system it came from.
entries.source: Investor Overview + Technical Whitepaper, canonical data model

entries.title: What makes SMPL different
entries.answer: Three things, by design and not as features bolted on: consistent results — the same inputs always produce the same outputs; transparent by design — every conclusion traces to underlying evidence and uncertainty is flagged, not hidden; and institutional knowledge — we preserve how your organization defines and measures its business and reproduce any report exactly as it was originally delivered.

entries.title: Adapts to your process
topics: do we have to change our process
how do you handle our ARR definition
keywords: do we have to change our process
how do you handle our arr definition
entries.answer: SMPL adapts to your finance organization instead of asking you to adapt to the software. You keep your definition of ARR, your forecasting methodology, and the board metrics your leadership already understands — the platform learns them once and automates them. Methodology is configuration the engine executes, not hardcoded logic, so the engine is the same for every customer but your configuration is yours.

entries.title: Deterministic calculations
entries.answer: Every calculation is deterministic: given the same inputs and methodology configuration, the engine returns the identical output on every run. The mechanism is versioning, not caching — each calculation runs against a specific timestamped snapshot. A report generated in March, reproduced today, reads exactly as it did in March, even if the underlying data was later corrected. Both the old and new views are correct; they answer 'what did we know then' versus 'what do we know now.'

entries.title: Evidence and explainability
topics: can you back up the numbers
keywords: can you back up the numbers
entries.answer: Every number traces to the specific source records that produced it — an invoice, an opportunity, a GL entry — not just an intermediate total. Explanations are generated the same way: a statement like 'expansion ARR beat forecast by $420K, driven by three enterprise upsells that closed early' comes from those three actual opportunity records, not a template. If the data doesn't support a specific explanation, the platform says so rather than inventing a plausible-sounding one.

entries.title: Confidence signals on numbers
entries.answer: Every number and explanation carries an explicit confidence signal. A value from complete, well-structured data reads high-confidence; a value derived by inference — say, ARR estimated from invoice history rather than an explicit contract record — reads visibly lower, with a note on what would resolve it. Confidence is never collapsed into false certainty in either direction.

entries.title: Period close governance
entries.answer: Each reporting period moves through an explicit close workflow. Once a period is finalized, corrections do not rewrite history — they are recorded as new dated entries that supersede the previous ones. That way you can always answer what the numbers were when leadership made a decision, versus what they are after a correction.

entries.title: Period close governance (internal deep)
entries.answer: Each reporting period moves through an explicit workflow: load, validate, lock, freeze, report. Once frozen, a period doesn't reopen — a correction is recorded as a new dated entry linked to the one it supersedes, producing a new snapshot going forward while the original stays intact. That's what makes 'what did we know, and when did we know it' an answerable question rather than an aspiration.

entries.title: vs Cube
topics: how do you compare to Cube
keywords: how do you compare to cube
entries.answer: Cube serves a similar buyer, and its AI messaging now sounds like ours on paper. The difference is architectural: Cube's core product is a bi-directional Excel and Sheets sync — the finance team still builds and maintains the model in spreadsheets, and Cube's AI makes that faster. That architecture can't guarantee deterministic calculations or board decks that reproduce exactly after a restatement. Cube makes a team faster at the work; we do the work and hand the team a defensible result to review.

entries.title: vs QuickBooks / incumbents
entries.answer: Incumbent accounting platforms are shipping AI variance analysis and commentary, and they'll keep closing surface-level feature gaps. Our durable advantage isn't a feature checklist — it's a data architecture built natively for SaaS metrics like ARR waterfalls, NRR and GRR, and quota ramp curves, with determinism and evidence attached by design, not general-ledger AI bolted on after the fact.

entries.title: vs Rillet
topics: how do you compare to Rillet
keywords: how do you compare to rillet
entries.answer: Rillet isn't a competitor — it replaces the system of record, while we supply the intelligence layer that sits above it and any other general ledger. We actually see a natural, complementary partnership opportunity there and are pursuing it.

entries.title: Target market / ICP
entries.answer: High-growth SaaS companies in roughly the $5 million to $50 million ARR range — the band where finance complexity first outpaces finance headcount, where companies first build a real FP&A function and first outgrow QuickBooks and spreadsheets at the same time. There are more than 27,000 SaaS companies in the US alone.

entries.title: Market growth
entries.answer: Estimates of the FP&A software market range from roughly $5 to $9 billion today, and nearly all of them agree on the direction: double-digit growth driven by the shift from spreadsheet-based planning to AI-native platforms. MGI Research puts cloud FP&A at nearly $8.5 billion in 2026, growing 28 percent year over year.

entries.title: Business impact / ROI
topics: how much time do you save
keywords: how much time do you save
entries.answer: Four things. Speed — reporting that takes weeks after close is done in minutes once data is loaded. Effort — a single ARR reporting package can consume 40 to 80 hours of finance time today, and we automate most of it. Confidence — every deliverable ships with the data behind it, reviewed before it's shared. Alignment — finance, leadership, and the board work from one trusted view instead of reconciling spreadsheets.

entries.title: Business model
entries.answer: A subscription platform sold directly to finance leadership, with a land-and-expand motion: customers start with core financial reporting and close automation, then expand into GTM efficiency, workforce modeling, and scenario planning as trust builds. Go-to-market runs through direct outreach to CFOs and VPs of Finance, plus partnerships with modern accounting platforms and advisory firms that reach the same buyer warmer than cold outbound.

entries.title: Where we are / traction
entries.answer: Platform design is complete — every data connection, calculation, and control is fully specified — and we can demonstrate it today on realistic SaaS data. We're not yet live with paying customers, which is exactly why we're bringing in a small number of design partners first, to validate against real data and shape the roadmap ahead of general availability.
entries.source: Executive Summary / Investor Overview, Where we are

entries.title: Implementation and security
entries.answer: Implementation integrates with your existing systems, typically over four to six weeks, delivered as a secure browser-based application — nothing to install, no infrastructure to manage. Data is encrypted in transit and at rest, with role-based access control from full GL-level access for finance down to summary, explained views for the board.
entries.source: Executive Summary, Where we are + Technical Whitepaper, Implementation

entries.title: Team / founder
topics: why are you the one to build this
keywords: why are you the one to build this
entries.answer: It's being built by a founder who has run the SaaS finance function directly — forecasting, opex management, management reporting, go-to-market reporting — alongside the data architecture and systems integration work underneath it. That combination is uncommon, and it's why the core architecture was designed by someone who's personally hit every failure mode of the spreadsheet-and-disconnected-systems status quo.
